scenes.text: At the surface, the ocean seems to have no end.
scenes.hero: The open ocean surface, horizon to horizon
scenes.camera: 40 m above the sea on the trench axis, 34 km from Challenger Deep; slow forward drift toward the horizon; pitch eases from -8° to -30° (looking down at the water) by the end of the line.
scenes.event: Low silver-blue sun, gentle swell; no other object in frame. The tilt down anticipates the dive.
scenes.visual_goal: Endless ocean from just above the surface.

scenes.text: But beneath the western Pacific, the seafloor drops into a world nearly eleven kilometres down.
scenes.hero: The trench cut into the seabed, revealed as one immense cross-section
scenes.camera: Plunges through the surface just after 'beneath', pitching to look straight down; descends to ~2,500 m while travelling along the trench axis toward Challenger Deep, then raises its gaze down the trench.
scenes.event: On 'seafloor' the seabed fades in below as a sonar-style relief; the trench opens beneath the camera by 'down'.
scenes.visual_goal: Dive through the surface; the trench is revealed below.

scenes.text: This is Challenger Deep, inside the Mariana Trench: the deepest known point in the ocean, measured at about ten thousand nine hundred thirty-five metres.
scenes.hero: The deepest basin of the trench, ringed by one bathymetric contour
scenes.camera: Glide down the trench axis from ~2,500 m to ~5,600 m (still above the hadal zone), looking ahead at the deepest basin.
scenes.event: Depth contours glow on the trench relief; one ring is drawn around the deepest basin starting on 'Challenger'; the basin floor brightens slightly on 'ten'.
scenes.visual_goal: Bathymetric view of the trench; the deepest basin is marked.

scenes.text: Sunlight vanishes far above it. Below six thousand metres lies the hadal zone:
scenes.hero: A single narrow beam of sunlight, far above, fading to black
scenes.camera: Tilts up toward the distant surface during the first sentence, then tilts back down and keeps descending into the trench.
scenes.event: The beam dims to nothing by the end of 'above it'; on 'six thousand' the 6,000 m contour glows once along the trench walls and recedes as the camera passes below it.
scenes.visual_goal: Last light from above disappears; crossing into the hadal zone.

scenes.text: near-freezing, pitch-dark, under pressure more than a thousand times the air at sea level.
scenes.hero: The pressure gauge on a descending research lander
scenes.camera: Catches up with a descending lander in total darkness and slides past its gauge in a close three-quarter view.
scenes.event: The sonar relief is gone: only the lander's lamps light the water. The gauge needle sweeps once to its high end on 'thousand'.
scenes.visual_goal: Pitch-dark water; the only light is the lander; the gauge reads extreme pressure.

scenes.text: And still, life persists. Small animals inhabit these trenches, surviving in the darkness.
scenes.hero: Pale hadal amphipods drifting into the lander's light
scenes.camera: Settles beside the lander's bait bag and slowly circles it.
scenes.event: From 'life' onward, small pale amphipods swim in from the dark toward the bait. No bioluminescence; they are seen only where the lamp reaches.
scenes.visual_goal: Small crustaceans gather in the lamp light.

scenes.text: The deepest fish ever filmed was found higher up, at eight thousand three hundred thirty-six metres, in another Pacific trench.
scenes.hero: One snailfish gliding through the light
scenes.camera: Holds level while one translucent snailfish crosses the lamp light, then tilts down as the lander continues its descent.
scenes.event: The fish enters on 'fish' and glides past in slow tail beats; it leaves the light before the line ends, staying well above the trench floor.
scenes.visual_goal: A single snailfish; labelled as a record from a different trench.

scenes.text: At the bottom, our maps are still incomplete. Earth's deepest frontier is not another planet. It's beneath us.
scenes.hero: The dark, vast floor of Challenger Deep
scenes.camera: Follows the lander down to the floor; after touchdown it slowly pulls back and rises, so the lander's pool of light becomes a small island in the dark. (Change from the draft plan's 'forward drift' — pending owner approval.)
scenes.event: The floor emerges from black on 'bottom'; the lander settles in its own light; the darkness around it grows as the camera withdraws.
scenes.visual_goal: Arrival on the deepest floor; quiet scale.

claims.text: Challenger Deep lies beneath the western Pacific Ocean, at the southern end of the Mariana Trench.
Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, is the deepest known point in the ocean.
Its depth was measured at about 10,935 m (Greenaway et al. 2021: 10,935 m ± 6 m at 95% confidence, below mean sea level, from June 2020 submersible transects) — i.e. nearly 11 km.
claims.note: Uncertainty: published estimates differ by method and survey (WHOI's hub cites 10,911 m; a 2010 mapping estimate was 10,984 m; Kobayashi 2012 cites 10,994 m). Narration says 'about'; on-screen figure follows NOAA and Greenaway et al.

claims.text: Sunlight does not reach the trench: ocean depths greater than 1,000 m are completely devoid of sunlight.
Trench depths below 6,000 m make up the hadal zone.
Hadal trenches are near-freezing ('constant temperatures just above freezing'), have no light, and pressures more than 1,000 times the surface (up to ~115 MPa at Challenger Deep).
claims.note: Not citing NOAA 'deep ocean' page for pressure: its '40 to over 110 times' range appears inconsistent with ~1,100 atm at ~11 km.

claims.text: Small animals live in hadal trenches, including the amphipod Hirondellea gigas, a resident of the Challenger Deep floor.

The deepest fish ever filmed is a snailfish (genus Pseudoliparis, species unidentified) at 8,336 m in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench (filmed 2022, announced April 2023) — not in Challenger Deep, and above Challenger Deep's depth.
The seafloor remains incompletely mapped: about 26% had been mapped in high resolution as of June 2024.
claims.note: Supports the general statement. Challenger Deep itself has been mapped at high resolution (multibeam); the narration line should be read as the deep seafloor in general — flagged for owner review.
